facts.statement: Articulated body fossils of Ctenoptychius apicalis were first described from the North Staffordshire Coalfield in 1890.
facts.quote: Articulated body fossils of Ctenoptychius apicalis were described from the North Staffordshire Coalfield in 1890.

facts.statement: The holotype tooth of the type species C. apicalis is currently missing.
facts.quote: The holotype tooth of C. apicalis is now missing.

facts.statement: Ctenoptychius is an extinct genus of cartilaginous fish belonging to the order Petalodontiformes, named for its 'comb-folded' appearance.
facts.quote: Ctenoptychius ('comb-folded', from the Greek κτείς kteís 'comb' and πτυχή ptychos 'fold') is an extinct genus of cartilaginous fish in the order Petalodontiformes.

facts.statement: C. apicalis is known mainly from flattened, serrated teeth, though some poorly preserved specimens show the head, pectoral fins, and body scales.
facts.quote: C. apicalis is known primarily from teeth, which have a flattened shape and serrated edges, although poorly-preserved specimens preserving the head, pectoral fins and scales of the body are also known.

facts.statement: Based on available fossils, Ctenoptychius is believed to have had a flattened, ray-like body.
facts.quote: Based on this, it is believed that Ctenoptychius had a flattened, ray-like body.

facts.statement: The tooth crowns of C. apicalis featured between three and nine small cusp-like structures called cusplets, with the central one being the largest.
facts.quote: The tooth crowns of Ctenoptychius apicalis had between three and nine small cusp-like structures termed cusplets, with the centermost being the largest.

facts.statement: The body of Ctenoptychius was depressiform (flattened) with large, broad pectoral fins.
facts.quote: The body of Ctenoptychius was depressiform and the pectoral fins were large and broad.

facts.statement: Fossils suggest Ctenoptychius lived in shallow marine environments and likely fed as an omnivorous bottom feeder on hard-shelled invertebrates.
facts.quote: Petalodont fossils are known primarily from shallow marine environments, and the stomach contents of Janassa imply that at least some members of the group were omnivorous bottom feeders that targeted hard-shelled invertebrates.

facts.statement: C. apicalis lived during the Late Carboniferous period, with fossils found in the United Kingdom and potentially the United States.
facts.quote: This species lived during the Late Carboniferous period, and its fossils are known from the United Kingdom and potentially the United States.

facts.statement: The genus Ctenoptychius existed from the Serpukhovian to the Kungurian stages, between 330.3 and 274.4 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Serpukhovian to Kungurian (330.3 to 274.4 million years ago)

facts.statement: Ctenoptychius belongs to the family Belantseidae.
Ctenoptychius is classified within the class Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fish).
The status of C. korni is debated; it has been assigned to Ctenoptychius or Janassa, but some researchers suggest it belongs to neither genus due to lacking distinctive features of both.
facts.quote: The taxon "Ctenoptychius" korni is known from complete, articulated body fossils from the Late Permian-age Kupferschiefer of Germany. This species has variously been assigned to Ctenoptychius and the distantly related genus Janassa, but has alternatively been suggested to belong to neither due to lacking the distinctive features of both genera.
